Against the Right to Be Forgotten: Why the Historical Record Must Remain Intact

Introduction

In 2014, the Court of Justice of the European Union handed down a ruling in Google Spain SL v. Agencia Española de Protección de Datos that fundamentally altered the relationship between individuals, information, and the internet. The court held that individuals could compel search engines to dereference links to accurate, lawfully published information about themselves — not because the information was false, not because it was obtained illegally, but simply because the subject found it inconvenient or embarrassing. The so-called "Right to Be Forgotten" (RTBF) has since spread through European data protection law, been codified in the General Data Protection Regulation, and inspired similar proposals worldwide.

It represents one of the most consequential and poorly reasoned expansions of censorship power in democratic history.

This essay argues directly and without qualification: the Right to Be Forgotten is a dangerous, philosophically incoherent, and practically destructive legal doctrine. It subordinates the public interest in accurate historical information to the private interest in personal reputation management. It empowers individuals — including powerful ones — to selectively erase inconvenient truths. It undermines journalism, scholarship, accountability, and the fundamental architecture of a free information society. The solution is not reform of RTBF but its abolition.

Part One: The Philosophical Incoherence of a Right to Erase Truth

1.1 Rights Claims Require Coherent Foundations

Rights, in liberal democratic theory, are not arbitrary preferences elevated to legal status. They require philosophical grounding — a demonstration that the interest being protected is sufficiently fundamental and that protecting it does not systematically violate the comparable interests of others. The right to free speech rests on the foundational importance of individual autonomy, political participation, and the collective pursuit of truth. The right to privacy protects bodily integrity and the capacity for self-development free from surveillance and intrusion.

The Right to Be Forgotten, by contrast, rests on the claim that individuals have a legitimate interest in controlling how others perceive and remember them — and that this interest is so significant it can override accurate, publicly relevant information. This is not a privacy right in any traditional sense. Traditional privacy protects information that was never legitimately public: medical records, private communications, sexual behavior conducted in private. The RTBF goes dramatically further. It claims the power to suppress information that was legitimately made public, that is accurate, and that remains potentially relevant to others.

This is not a privacy right. It is a reputation management right — a legal entitlement to control one's public image by suppressing inconvenient facts. And unlike genuine privacy rights, it cannot be exercised without actively harming others: journalists who reported the truth, archives that preserved it, citizens who might wish to access it.

1.2 Truth Is Not the Property of Its Subject

There is a fundamental category error at the heart of RTBF thinking: the confusion between information about a person and information belonging to a person. When a court convicts someone of fraud, that conviction is a public fact. When a politician makes a controversial speech, that speech is a public fact. When a business executive is dismissed for misconduct, that dismissal — if publicly reported — is a public fact. These events occurred in the world. They were witnessed, documented, reported upon. They are part of the historical record.

RTBF doctrine implicitly treats such facts as belonging, in some meaningful sense, to the person they concern — as if the subject of information has a proprietary claim over its continued circulation. But this is incoherent. Facts are not intellectual property. A convicted fraudster does not own the record of his conviction. A disgraced politician does not own the reporting about her misconduct. A company that dumped toxic waste does not own the environmental records documenting its behavior.

To grant individuals property-like rights over facts about themselves is to fundamentally distort the nature of information and history. Facts do not belong to the people they describe. They belong, if they belong to anyone, to the record of human events — to history, to journalism, to the collective memory that allows societies to function, learn, and hold power accountable.

1.3 The "Outdated Information" Fiction

Proponents of RTBF frequently invoke the concept of "outdated" or "irrelevant" information — the idea that decades-old records are no longer pertinent and that their continued accessibility constitutes an ongoing harm disproportionate to any public benefit. This argument sounds superficially reasonable but dissolves under examination.

The question of what information is "relevant" is inherently contested and context-dependent. A DUI conviction from 1995 might seem irrelevant in 2024 — unless the person is now seeking to become a commercial airline pilot, or running for a position involving public safety, or has publicly claimed a decades-long commitment to sobriety. A bankruptcy from the 1980s might seem ancient history — unless the person is now managing large amounts of other people's money. An old lawsuit might seem forgettable — unless the defendant is now in a position of power where the pattern of behavior documented in that lawsuit is directly relevant.

Who decides what is "relevant"? Under RTBF regimes, the answer is ultimately the person who benefits most from suppression — the subject of the information. This is an extraordinary conflict of interest built directly into the legal structure. The person with the strongest motivation to hide information is given decisive authority over whether it remains accessible. The result is not a careful balancing of public and private interests; it is systematic bias toward concealment.

Part Two: The Threat to Democratic Accountability

2.1 Public Figures and the Accountability Deficit

Perhaps the most immediate and obvious harm caused by RTBF laws is their use by powerful individuals to suppress legitimate accountability journalism. The European RTBF framework nominally excludes matters of "public interest" and allows exceptions for "journalism" and "historical research." In practice, these exceptions are inadequate, contested, and routinely circumvented.

Consider the cases that have actually emerged under European RTBF requests. Politicians have sought to dereference articles documenting their past statements and positions. Executives have sought to remove reporting about corporate misconduct. Individuals convicted of serious crimes have successfully forced the removal of links to contemporary news coverage of their prosecutions. In one widely discussed case, a doctor sought to remove links to accurate reports about his negligence. In another, a former member of the Nazi party sought the suppression of historical records.

These are not edge cases. They are the predictable consequence of giving individuals the unilateral power to suppress accurate information about themselves. Power will always be the primary beneficiary of information suppression. Those with resources to hire lawyers, navigate bureaucratic processes, and pressure platforms are overwhelmingly more likely to exercise RTBF rights than private individuals genuinely harmed by casual cruelty. The law in practice operates as a reputation laundering service disproportionately available to the wealthy and powerful.

Democratic accountability requires that the public have persistent access to accurate information about those who hold power. A politician who supported a disastrous policy deserves to have that support documented. An executive who oversaw corporate fraud deserves to have that fraud reported. A judge who made a biased ruling deserves to have that ruling preserved in accessible form. The moment we allow these individuals to suppress this information — even years or decades later — we fundamentally compromise the informational infrastructure that democracy requires.

2.2 The Chilling Effect on Journalism

The harm to journalism extends beyond specific suppression cases. The existence of RTBF liability creates a chilling effect on the entire enterprise of investigative and archival journalism. When publications know that any story they publish — regardless of its accuracy, its newsworthiness, its public importance — can subsequently be ordered removed from search engine results and potentially from their own archives, the incentive structure for journalism shifts.

Stories about private individuals, even when clearly in the public interest, become liability risks. Archiving becomes legally precarious. Building comprehensive databases of historical reporting — the kind of searchable historical record that allows modern journalists to identify patterns, track behavior over time, and provide context for current events — becomes an activity fraught with legal risk.

This is not a theoretical concern. European news organizations have faced exactly these pressures since 2014. The practical effect is a two-tiered information environment: current reporting remains largely available, but historical reporting — the context and record that gives current events meaning — becomes progressively harder to access as RTBF requests accumulate over time. This is precisely the wrong direction. If anything, the searchability and accessibility of historical journalism is one of the most valuable features of the digital age, allowing citizens to contextualize and verify claims in ways that were previously impossible.

2.3 Institutional Memory and Pattern Recognition

Beyond individual accountability, RTBF laws threaten the capacity of institutions, researchers, and the public to identify patterns of behavior over time. Much of what makes the digital archive valuable is precisely its comprehensiveness. A single report of misconduct might be ambiguous. Ten reports, from different sources, spanning years, constitute a pattern. That pattern might be the difference between recognizing a serial predator and dismissing a single complaint.

The #MeToo movement demonstrated with extraordinary clarity how crucial it is that historical reporting about misconduct remains accessible. In case after case, the critical mass of evidence against powerful abusers was assembled only because decades of reporting — some of it apparently forgotten, some of it dismissed as isolated incidents — remained accessible and searchable. RTBF laws would have allowed many of these individuals to progressively suppress this historical record, making the pattern harder to recognize and the eventual accountability less likely.

The same logic applies to corporate misconduct, financial fraud, political corruption, and institutional abuse. The ability to connect historical dots — to see that the company now seeking a government contract was previously found guilty of fraud, that the charity director now soliciting donations was previously investigated for financial misconduct, that the political candidate making certain promises previously broke those same promises in office — depends on a comprehensive, accessible historical record. RTBF systematically degrades that record.

Part Three: The Practical Failures of RTBF Implementation

3.1 The Streisand Effect and Technological Futility

RTBF laws are not merely harmful in principle; they are frequently ineffective in practice. The famous "Streisand Effect" — named for Barbara Streisand's ill-fated attempt to suppress aerial photographs of her property, which resulted in far greater publicity than the original images ever achieved — applies with particular force to RTBF requests. When a notable RTBF request becomes public, the resulting coverage often makes the suppressed information far more widely known than it would otherwise have been.

More broadly, RTBF laws operate against the fundamental architecture of the internet, which was designed for information redundancy and resilience. When a link is dereferenced from Google's European search results, the underlying information typically remains accessible through other search engines, through direct URL access, through archive services like the Wayback Machine, through mirror sites, through social media, and through countless other channels. The practical effect is not suppression but inconvenience — the information is harder to find for casual searchers while remaining readily accessible to anyone with moderate technical sophistication.

This creates a deeply inequitable information environment. RTBF laws are most effective against the least sophisticated users — ordinary citizens who rely on conventional search engines. Researchers, journalists, determined members of the public, foreign observers, and anyone using a VPN to access non-European search results will typically be unaffected. The laws create an illusion of suppression while delivering actual suppression primarily against the most casual and least powerful categories of information-seekers.

3.2 The Administrative Opacity Problem

RTBF systems operate with minimal transparency. Google and other search engines receive RTBF requests, make determinations about which to honor, and implement those determinations largely outside public view. There is no comprehensive public record of what has been suppressed, who requested the suppression, or what rationale was given. The entities making these decisions — private corporations operating under regulatory pressure — have neither the expertise, the independence, nor the accountability appropriate for decisions with such significant public consequences.

This opacity is not incidental; it is structurally inherent to how RTBF operates. The entire premise is that information should be suppressed quietly — that the subject of a suppression request is entitled not merely to have information removed but to have the removal itself remain invisible. The result is a systematic invisible editing of the public record that citizens cannot evaluate, journalists cannot scrutinize, and researchers cannot study.

When governments want to censor information in traditional contexts, they do so through transparent legal processes — court orders, regulatory findings, legislative action — that can be challenged, appealed, and criticized. RTBF operates through an administrative apparatus that is simultaneously privately operated, publicly mandated, and fundamentally opaque. It is censorship without accountability, erasure without transparency.

3.3 The Scope Creep Problem

RTBF laws were originally justified by reference to relatively sympathetic scenarios: the young person whose minor criminal conviction continued to follow them years after rehabilitation, the victim of online harassment whose attackers' lies continued to circulate, the private individual whose personal information had been aggregated and weaponized. Even granting these justifications arguendo, the laws as implemented have expanded far beyond these scenarios.

The categorical structure of RTBF — a general right with specific exceptions, rather than a specific right with general limitations — creates inevitable pressure toward expansion. Each new interpretation of "relevance," each new judicial decision about what constitutes legitimate "public interest," potentially expands the range of suppressible information. The trajectory of RTBF law since 2014 has consistently moved toward broader individual rights and narrower public interest exceptions.

This is not surprising. The political economy of RTBF creates systematic pressure toward expansion. Individuals who want information suppressed are motivated, organized, and legally represented. The diffuse public interest in maintaining historical records is not represented by any organized constituency in RTBF proceedings. Over time, this asymmetry reliably produces expansion of suppression rights and erosion of public interest protections.

Part Four: Responding to the Arguments for RTBF

4.1 The Rehabilitation Argument

The most emotionally compelling argument for RTBF is the rehabilitation argument: that individuals who have genuinely changed deserve the opportunity for a fresh start, and that the permanent accessibility of past mistakes prevents rehabilitation and reintegration. A person convicted of a crime, having served their sentence, should not be defined forever by their worst moment. A young person who made a foolish public statement should not have that statement follow them for decades.

This argument deserves genuine engagement — not dismissal. The human interest in moving past one's mistakes is real and sympathetic. The concern that the internet creates a permanent record that eliminates the natural fading of memory is legitimate.

But the rehabilitation argument does not support RTBF laws. It supports, at most, thoughtful design of criminal records systems, statutes of limitations for civil liability, and social norms about the appropriateness of raising old matters. It does not support the active suppression of accurate historical information.

The reason is straightforward: rehabilitation does not require that others forget. It requires that the rehabilitated individual be extended opportunities, courtesy, and the benefit of the doubt despite a difficult history. These are matters of social practice and individual judgment, not matters that law can or should mandate by forcing others to be ignorant. A future employer who knows about a past conviction and still chooses to hire someone is extending genuine grace. An employer who hires someone in ignorance of relevant history has not exercised judgment at all — they have been denied the information needed to exercise it.

Moreover, the rehabilitation argument is self-defeating in a crucial respect. Genuine rehabilitation is most convincing when it is visible against the background of the original behavior. A person who can say, "Yes, I did that, and here is how I have changed and what I have done since" makes a far more compelling case than a person whose record has been quietly erased. RTBF allows the performance of rehabilitation without its substance — the appearance of a clean record without the actual work of redemption.

4.2 The Contextual Integrity Argument

A more sophisticated argument for RTBF draws on philosopher Helen Nissenbaum's concept of "contextual integrity" — the idea that information flows appropriately when they match the norms of the context in which information was originally shared. A person who made a statement in a local newspaper in 1995 shared it in a context with limited geographical reach and effective temporal limits (newspapers are not typically archived accessibly for decades). Making that statement globally and permanently searchable violates the norms of the original context, the argument goes, even if it was technically public.

This argument has some intuitive appeal but fails on examination. First, it proves too much: by this logic, any digitization of historical records — any searchable database of court records, any accessible newspaper archive, any online collection of historical documents — potentially violates contextual norms, since the original context did not include global digital accessibility. This would mean that the entire project of making historical information accessible online is normatively problematic, a conclusion that cannot be seriously maintained.

Second, contextual integrity is a descriptive concept about information norms, not a normative principle that should override other considerations. Some contextual norms deserve to be preserved; others do not. The contextual norm of the small town where everyone knows the victim's name in a rape case does not deserve preservation. The contextual norm of corporate secrecy that keeps regulatory violations private does not deserve preservation. Whether a particular contextual norm should be legally enforced requires substantive argument, not simply the observation that norms exist.

Third, the argument ignores the legitimate interests of those who might benefit from accessible historical information — future potential victims of a predator, future voters considering a politician's record, future employers or clients of a professional with a history of misconduct. Their interests in accessing relevant information are as legitimate as the subject's interest in not having it easily found.

4.3 The "Digital Permanence Creates New Harms" Argument

Proponents of RTBF sometimes argue that the digital age has created genuinely new forms of harm that require new legal responses. Pre-internet, information naturally faded: newspaper archives required physical effort to access, social memory was limited by human cognitive constraints, and the practical inaccessibility of historical information provided de facto protection against the indefinite salience of past events. The internet eliminates this natural fading, creating a form of permanent record that is qualitatively different from what preceded it and that may produce real psychological and social harms.

This is empirically plausible as a description of changed information conditions. But the proposed remedy is disproportionate and misdirected. The response to the changed information environment should be changes in social norms — in how employers, courts, insurers, and individuals weigh historical information — not changes in the historical record itself. We should be developing social and legal frameworks that prevent historical information from being used in unduly punitive ways (for instance, by limiting how old convictions can be used in employment decisions), not frameworks that suppress the information itself.

The analogy to human memory is instructive here. Human memory fades not because the events never happened or because others are forbidden from remembering them, but because of cognitive limitations. We do not have a "right to be forgotten" in human memory — others are legally and morally permitted to remember our past actions. What we have, informally, is the practical likelihood that memories will fade. The appropriate response to the internet's elimination of this practical likelihood is not to create a legal right that mimics cognitive forgetting but to develop mature social practices for dealing with a world in which information persists.

Part Five: What Should Be Done Instead

5.1 Strengthen Traditional Privacy Protections

The legitimate concerns that motivate RTBF advocacy — protection of genuinely private information, prevention of doxxing and harassment, control over sensitive personal data — are better addressed through targeted privacy protections that do not threaten the public historical record. Strong rules protecting genuinely private information (medical records, private communications, location data, financial details) from unauthorized publication, combined with robust remedies for defamation and harassment, address the most serious harms without creating general rights to suppress accurate public information.

The key distinction is between information that was legitimately private and has been improperly exposed — which genuinely warrants legal protection — and information that was properly public and remains accurate — which does not. Traditional privacy law largely respects this distinction. RTBF law abandons it.

5.2 Reform Criminal Records Systems

Much of the genuine humanitarian concern behind RTBF relates specifically to criminal records — the worry that people who have served their sentences and reformed continue to be defined by past convictions. This is a real problem, but it should be addressed directly through criminal records reform: expanding expungement eligibility, limiting the circumstances in which old convictions can be considered in employment and housing decisions, reforming sex offender registries, and developing clear legal frameworks for what employers and institutions can consider in background checks.

These reforms target the actual harm — the use of old convictions to prevent rehabilitation — without creating a general right to suppress accurate historical information. They address the problem of criminal records by changing how records can be used, not by pretending the underlying events did not happen.

5.3 Develop Mature Digital Literacy and Social Norms

Ultimately, the most important response to concerns about digital permanence is cultural rather than legal. Societies need to develop mature norms for how historical information is weighted — recognizing that a twenty-year-old record is not necessarily a reliable guide to current character, that people change, that context matters, and that the existence of information does not require its indefinite salience. This is a project for education, journalism, and social practice, not for law.

Legal interventions that try to force a particular relationship with historical information by suppressing it are both disproportionate and ineffective. They treat the symptom — the accessibility of information — rather than the disease — the failure to develop wise practices for using it.

Conclusion: The Historical Record as Democratic Infrastructure

The Right to Be Forgotten is not, at its core, a privacy right. It is a censorship right — a legally enforceable power to suppress accurate information that its subject finds inconvenient. Dressed in the language of dignity and autonomy, it operates in practice as a tool for reputation management by the powerful, a structural threat to journalism and accountability, and a systematic corruption of the historical record that democratic societies depend upon.

The historical record is not merely an academic curiosity or a technological artifact. It is democratic infrastructure — the accumulated documentation of events, decisions, and behavior that allows citizens to hold power accountable, that allows institutions to learn from experience, that allows individuals to make informed judgments about the people and organizations they interact with. Every suppression request that is honored is a small erasure from this record, and the cumulative effect of millions of such erasures, over years and decades, is the progressive degradation of the informational commons.

The answer to the genuine problems of digital permanence, online harassment, and the misuse of historical information is not to give individuals the power to edit history in their favor. It is to build stronger protections for genuinely private information, reform systems that misuse public records, and develop the social maturity to engage wisely with a world in which information persists. These are hard things to do. They require sustained effort across legal, cultural, and technological domains.

But they are the right things to do. Erasing the past is always the easier choice — for the powerful, for those with something to hide, for those who would rather not be judged by their history. It is not the choice that a free, democratic, and truth-respecting society should make. The Right to Be Forgotten should be forgotten — honestly, without legal compulsion, because the argument for it cannot withstand scrutiny.

The truth does not owe anyone oblivion.

This essay presents arguments against Right to Be Forgotten legislation from a free speech, democratic accountability, and historical preservation perspective. It does not address every legitimate concern about digital privacy, and readers are encouraged to engage with scholarly literature on both sides of this debate, including work by Viktor Mayer-Schönberger, Jeffrey Rosen, Paul Bernal, and others.

"The Permanence of Truth: A Defense of Memory"

A Speech Against 'Right to Be Forgotten' Policies

Ladies and gentlemen, fellow citizens, defenders of an open society:

We stand today at a crossroads between two competing visions of human civilization. One vision says that the past belongs to those who lived it, and that individuals may reach backward through time and selectively erase what embarrasses, inconveniences, or implicates them. The other vision — the one I will defend with every argument at my disposal — says that truth, once recorded, belongs to everyone.

I am here to argue passionately, forcefully, and without apology that so-called "Right to Be Forgotten" policies represent one of the most dangerous ideas to gain mainstream legal legitimacy in our lifetimes. And I intend to tell you exactly why.

I. The Historical Stakes Are Not Theoretical

Let us begin with the most uncomfortable truth available to us.

History is not a collection of abstract facts. History is a warning system. It tells us which politicians defrauded their constituents, which executives poisoned their communities, which institutions covered up abuse, and which movements normalized atrocity before anyone recognized what was happening.

Every civilization that has experimented with the organized erasure of inconvenient information has paid a catastrophic price. The Index Librorum Prohibitorum. Stalin's doctored photographs. China's ongoing erasure of Tiananmen Square from its own internet. These are not distant cautionary tales. They are the logical endpoint of the principle that certain information is better forgotten.

I am not suggesting that a European court granting a delisting request is equivalent to Stalinist revisionism. I am suggesting they share a foundational premise: that someone in authority gets to decide which truths are too inconvenient to circulate freely.

Once you accept that premise, you have only a matter of degree separating democratic information management from authoritarian information control. The principle is identical. Only the power and the motivation differ — and both of those can change.

II. The Architecture of Accountability Is Being Dismantled

Consider what the Right to Be Forgotten actually does in practice.

A financial advisor who defrauded elderly clients files a request to delist news articles about his conviction. Granted.

A physician whose patients complained about negligence requests removal of those reviews and reports. Considered.

A politician who voted for a deeply unpopular policy during a crisis requests that contemporaneous reporting be suppressed from search results. Argued.

A corporate executive whose company dumped chemicals into a watershed requests that investigative journalism be effectively buried. Pursued.

This is not privacy protection. This is reputation laundering. And the people most capable of pursuing it are precisely those with the resources, the legal sophistication, and the motivation to do so — which means it disproportionately protects the powerful while the rest of us lose the tools to scrutinize them.

Accountability journalism, consumer protection research, background investigations, historical scholarship — all of these depend on the principle that documented facts remain accessible. When we begin granting individuals the authority to curate their own historical footprint, we are not protecting the vulnerable. We are arming the influential.

III. Privacy and Truth Are Not Opposites — But 'Forgotten' Policies Pretend They Are

I want to be direct about something, because intellectual honesty demands it: privacy is a genuine and important value. I am not standing here as an enemy of privacy. The teenage mistake, the youthful indiscretion, the personal medical information, the private communication — these deserve protection, and robust legal frameworks already exist to provide it.

But the Right to Be Forgotten, as constructed and applied, does not primarily protect people from having their private medical records exposed. It primarily protects people from having their public conduct remembered.

There is a profound moral difference between:

  • A private individual's personal struggle, which deserves discretion
  • A public figure's exercise of public power, which demands transparency

And there is an equally profound difference between:

  • Protecting information that was never legitimately public
  • Suppressing information that was legitimately reported and is genuinely relevant

Right to Be Forgotten policies consistently blur these distinctions, and they do so in ways that systematically favor those seeking erasure over those who depend on the information.

The person who committed financial fraud has an interest in being forgotten. The person considering hiring him as their accountant has a right to remember.

Whose interest should the law protect?

IV. The Search Engine Is Not the Problem

Advocates for these policies often frame their argument cleverly: they are not asking that information be deleted from the internet, only that it be delisted from search results. This sounds like a reasonable compromise. It is, in fact, a deliberate fiction.

In a world where information is discovered almost entirely through search, delisting is deletion in any practical sense. If a story cannot be found, it does not exist for the overwhelming majority of people who would benefit from knowing it. The distinction between "technically available" and "practically accessible" is not a legal technicality — it is the entire ballgame.

Furthermore, this framing puts search engines in an impossible position: they must become adjudicators of historical truth, deciding link by link, story by story, which documented facts are sufficiently current, relevant, or justified to remain in public view. This is an extraordinary editorial power, assigned not through democratic deliberation but through legal liability.

We should be deeply alarmed — not relieved — that we are outsourcing decisions about historical memory to corporate legal departments responding to individual complaints.

V. The Chilling Effect on Knowledge Itself

Let me speak now to journalists, historians, researchers, librarians, and educators — because this concerns you most directly.

Every field of human inquiry depends on the verifiability of sources and the persistence of records. When a news organization cannot be confident that its published investigation will remain publicly accessible, it faces pressure — subtle but real — to soften its conclusions, narrow its subjects, and avoid the most powerful targets, who are most likely to pursue erasure.

When a researcher studying patterns of institutional misconduct finds that key data points have been delisted, the analysis becomes incomplete. When a student fact-checking a political figure's claims finds that contemporaneous reporting has been suppressed, civic education is undermined.

It is the right to add information, to provide explanation, to ensure that the most recent and relevant facts appear alongside historical ones. Not the abuse survivor whose name was published without consent — existing privacy law protects them more directly.

Not the private individual who made a youthful mistake — proportionality standards and editorial discretion already address much of this.

The primary beneficiaries of robust Right to Be Forgotten enforcement are individuals and institutions with something documented, something public, and something they would rather you not know. The executives. The politicians. The institutions. The people with resources to pursue removal and motivation to achieve it.

Every time we allow a powerful person to erase documented history, we weaken every person who depends on that history to make informed decisions about their money, their vote, their safety, and their children.

The asymmetry is not accidental. It is inherent to the policy.

Choose memory over managed narrative. Choose a society in which documented truth persists, in which journalists can report without fear that their work will be erased by those it implicates, in which historians can reconstruct events without finding that inconvenient participants have disappeared from the record.

Choose a legal framework that protects genuine privacy — the private, the intimate, the irrelevant — while refusing to extend that protection to the public conduct of public figures and the documented consequences of real decisions.

Choose a democracy that trusts its citizens with information rather than one that increasingly decides, case by case, which truths are too much for us to handle.

The right to be forgotten is not a human right. The right to know is. The right to access documented history is. The right to make decisions based on verifiable information is.

And every one of those rights is diminished — measurably, consequentially, and often irreversibly — every time we allow the past to be edited by those with the power and motivation to do so.

History belongs to all of us, or it belongs to none of us.

Title: The Case Against 'Right to be Forgotten' Laws: Championing Unrestricted Access to Historical Online Information

Introduction

The 'Right to be Forgotten' (RTBF) laws, prominent in the European Union and other regions, enable individuals to request the removal of personal information from internet search results. While advocates argue that these laws help protect privacy and facilitate personal growth, this essay strongly contends that RTBF laws should be opposed. They infringe on freedom of expression, hinder access to historical records, and impede the transparency and accountability that are vital to a well-informed society.

1. Freedom of Expression and Information

RTBF laws clash with the fundamental right to freedom of expression and information. By allowing individuals to remove lawfully published content from search results, these laws essentially enable the rewriting of history. In a world where digital content is increasingly the primary source of information, RTBF laws can create blind spots, preventing access to accurate and comprehensive historical records (Rosen, 2012).

Moreover, RTBF laws set a dangerous precedent for censorship. They empower individuals to suppress lawful, truthful information, opening the door for potential misuse. Once such a right is established, it can be challenging to contain its application, leading to a chilling effect on free speech (Ambrose & Ausloos, 2017).

2. Transparency and Accountability

Unrestricted access to historical online information is crucial for maintaining transparency and accountability. RTBF laws can be exploited to obscure past misdeeds, making it difficult to hold individuals accountable for their actions. For instance, politicians or public figures could potentially misuse these laws to cleanse their online records, hindering the public's right to know (Fuster, 2010).

In addition, RTBF laws can undermine journalistic and academic work that relies on accurate historical records. They may interfere with investigative journalism, whistleblowing, and scholarly research, which depend on ready access to comprehensive information (Tombal, 2019).

3. Technical Challenges and Ineffectiveness

Implementing RTBF laws is fraught with technical challenges and can be ineffective. Information removed from one platform may still exist elsewhere on the internet or in physical archives. Furthermore, determining what links to remove requires complex, case-by-case assessments, which can be resource-intensive and inconsistent (Ausloos, 2018).

RTBF laws also struggle to strike a balance between privacy and the public interest. The internet is global, but these laws are local, leading to fragmented access to information and a "splinternet" effect, where access to information varies based on location (Mueller, 2017).

4. Alternatives to RTBF Laws

Instead of RTBF laws, efforts should focus on promoting digital literacy and responsible data handling practices. Individuals should have the skills to manage their online presence proactively, while publishers should adhere to ethical guidelines regarding the removal or updating of outdated or inaccurate information (Tene & Polonetsky, 2013).

Moreover, anonymization and pseudonymization techniques can help mitigate privacy concerns without resorting to censorship. These approaches allow historical records to remain intact while protecting individual privacy.

Conclusion

While RTBF laws are well-intentioned, they pose significant threats to freedom of expression, transparency, and accountability. Instead of legislating the removal of historical online information, societies should invest in digital literacy, ethical data practices, and privacy-enhancing technologies. By promoting these alternatives, we can strive for a balance between privacy and the right to information without resorting to censorship. The internet is a collective record of humanity's thoughts, actions, and experiences; we should preserve it as such, ensuring that our digital history remains accessible and intact for future generations.

When a court ruling, a news article, a police record, or a public statement is delisted from search results—not removed from existence, but effectively buried—it is treated as though relevance is a static condition determined by the subject of the information rather than by the public's ongoing need to access it.

Consider a concrete example. In the Costeja González case itself, the court ordered delisting of a 1998 notice announcing the auction of his property for the recovery of unpaid debts. The court deemed this information "irrelevant" in 2014. But the fact that a man owed debts in 1998 is not irrelevant—it is a historical event. Relevance is not a property of the fact itself; it is a function of the question being asked. For a financial historian researching the Spanish property crisis of the late 1990s, that auction notice is primary source material. For a neighbor researching property history before purchasing nearby real estate, that notice contains material information. For journalists investigating patterns of debt in specific regions during specific periods, that notice is evidence.

The right to be forgotten does not distinguish between these uses. It empowers the subject of the information to unilaterally determine that their personal inconvenience outweighs every possible public interest in continued access. This is not the work of a free press or an open archive. This is the work of a censor acting at the behest of the individual most motivated to suppress the truth.

When governments or courts permit this kind of historical editing, they implicitly adopt the position that the past belongs to those who lived it rather than to the collective memory of society. This is a philosophical error with practical consequences. A society that allows its members to sanitize their public records does not preserve dignity—it erodes accountability. It does not heal the past; it creates the illusion that the past never happened.

II. The Collapse of Accountability

The right to be forgotten poses a severe threat to public accountability, one of the foundational pillars of democratic governance.

Consider how this right operates in practice. When a public official has been convicted of corruption, and the news articles detailing that conviction are delisted from search results, future voters researching that official's background will find nothing. When a corporation has been found guilty of environmental contamination, and the scientific studies and regulatory findings are delisted, future consumers and regulators will lack access to that record. When a pattern of misconduct—a history of workplace harassment, fraud, or negligence—is scrubbed from public view, future potential victims lose access to information that could protect them.

Proponents of the right to be forgotten argue that these scenarios are addressed by exemptions for public figures and matters of public interest. But these exemptions are narrow, inconsistently applied, and deeply subjective. In the European framework, data protection authorities have granted delisting requests in cases involving criminal convictions, financial misconduct, and professional negligence—cases where any reasonable observer would argue that public interest in continued access is paramount.

The problem is structural. When an individual can request the suppression of information about their own wrongdoing, the burden of proof shifts. Instead of the public having a presumptive right to access truthful information about events that occurred, the default becomes suppression, with the burden falling on journalists, academics, or concerned citizens to demonstrate that the information is still "relevant." This inversion is fundamentally anti-democratic. In a functioning democracy, the flow of truthful information should require no justification. It is suppression that requires justification.

The right to be forgotten, as currently implemented, effectively creates a legal mechanism for the powerful and well-resourced to erase inconvenient histories. Those who can afford legal representation to process delisting requests can systematically bury their pasts, while those without resources—ordinary citizens, small business owners, individuals targeted by misinformation campaigns—lack the same ability. Far from being a universal right, the right to be forgotten functions as a privilege of the legally sophisticated.

III. The Chilling Effect on Journalism and Public Discourse

One of the most insidious consequences of the right to be forgotten is its chilling effect on journalists and the media.

When news organizations publish articles about crimes, scandals, or misconduct, those articles become part of the historical record. They are the product of investigative labor, legal vetting, and editorial oversight. When these articles are delisted from search results—not because they are factually wrong, but because the subject of the articles finds them embarrassing—the value of that journalistic work is destroyed.

News organizations do not exist to serve the comfort of the people they report on. They exist to inform the public. A journalist who writes about a company's environmental violations, or a politician's financial impropriety, or a pattern of institutional failures, performs a public service. When that article is effectively removed from the informational commons through delisting, the journalist's work is rendered invisible. The next time a similar story emerges, it will appear to be the first instance rather than part of a documented pattern. Institutional memory, which depends on the persistence of documentation, is degraded.

This dynamic creates perverse incentives. If journalists know that articles they publish today may be delisted in five years at the request of the subject, they face a diminished sense of the permanence—and therefore the significance—of their work. While journalists will not stop reporting, the degradation of the archive weakens the cumulative power of investigative journalism. Journalism is not merely about the present moment; it is about building a body of evidence over time. That body cannot be maintained if its individual components can be legally suppressed.

Furthermore, the right to be forgotten can function as a tool of intimidation. Public figures who have the resources to pursue delisting requests can signal to news organizations that reporting on their activities may ultimately be futile—that the resulting articles will be buried, stripped of their discoverability, and rendered functionally invisible. This is a form of indirect censorship that does not require a takedown notice or a prior restraint; it requires only the patient application of a legal right after the fact.

IV. The Impossibility of Coherent Application

Beyond its principled objections, the right to be forgotten suffers from a profound practical problem: it cannot be applied coherently.

The right as implemented operates through search engine delisting, not content removal. The original information remains online—in court databases, newspaper archives, government registries, and personal websites—but is removed from search results in specific jurisdictions. This creates a bizarre informational asymmetry. A piece of information does not cease to exist because it no longer appears in Google search results for European users. It still exists. It can still be found through direct URLs, alternative search engines, social media links, and other means. The right to be forgotten, in this sense, does not protect privacy—it creates a Potemkin privacy, a superficial erasure that leaves the underlying information entirely accessible to anyone willing to look beyond the dominant search engine.

This is not a minor technicality. It reveals the fundamental incoherence of the right as a privacy measure. If the goal is to protect an individual's dignity by preventing the public from accessing truthful information about their past, then the right fails: the information remains accessible. If the goal is merely to make that information harder to find, then the right is revealed to be not a privacy measure but an inconvenience measure—a legal tool for reducing the discoverability of embarrassing but truthful facts. The latter is not a compelling justification for state intervention in the informational commons.

Moreover, the right to be forgotten creates jurisdictional absurdities. An article delisted in the European Union remains fully discoverable in the United States, Asia, and elsewhere. An individual's "forgotten" past is available to anyone outside the delisting jurisdiction. This produces a world in which one's right to privacy varies by geography—a patchwork system that satisfies neither the demands of those who want comprehensive privacy nor the demands of those who want comprehensive access. It is a solution that pleases no one fully while creating administrative complexity for everyone.

The criteria for delisting are equally inconsistent. Data protection authorities in different EU member states have applied wildly different standards to similar requests. One authority might delist a news article about a criminal conviction while another refuses, depending on the nature of the crime, the time elapsed, and the subjective assessment of the authority. This inconsistency is not a minor flaw—it is a fundamental feature of a system that attempts to apply subjective relevance judgments to objective historical facts. There is no coherent principle that distinguishes a criminal conviction that should remain publicly discoverable from one that should be suppressed. The boundary is drawn not by law but by the discretionary judgment of the decision-maker.

V. The False Dichotomy: Privacy vs. the Right to Know

Proponents of the right to be forgotten frame the debate as a conflict between privacy and the right to know, with privacy as the morally superior value. This framing is both misleading and dangerous.

The right to privacy, properly understood, is a right against unreasonable intrusion into private life—the right to one's home, one's correspondence, one's inner thoughts. It is not, and has never historically been, a right to control the narrative of one's public actions. When an individual commits a crime, appears in a court proceeding, publishes a public statement, engages in professional misconduct, or participates in any other publicly observable event, the resulting record is not a violation of their privacy. It is a record of their public life. The right to privacy does not extend to the suppression of facts about one's conduct in the public sphere.

To treat truthful public records as privacy violations is to fundamentally redefine privacy in a way that privileges individual comfort over collective knowledge. It assumes that an individual's subjective sense of well-being is a higher-order value than the public's need to know what actually happened. This is not a balanced trade-off; it is a surrender.

The alternative vision—unrestricted access to historically available information—is not an assault on privacy. It is a commitment to the principle that truthful facts about public events should remain publicly accessible. This does not mean that individuals have no privacy rights; it means that privacy rights do not extend to the suppression of documented public facts. A person's private correspondence remains private. A person's medical records remain confidential. A person's personal diary remains unpublished. But a court ruling? A news article? A government record? These belong to the public. They were created to inform, and they must remain accessible to fulfill that purpose.

VI. The Precedent of State-Controlled Memory

Finally, the right to be forgotten must be evaluated in its historical context. Throughout human history, the power to control the written record has been the hallmark of authoritarian regimes. States that rewrite textbooks, burn archives, and suppress inconvenient documentation are recognized as threats to truth and liberty. The right to be forgotten, while implemented through legal rather than coercive means, represents a gentler form of the same impulse: the belief that the state should have the power to determine which facts about the past remain discoverable and which do not.

One need not be alarmist to recognize this pattern. The right to be forgotten establishes a legal framework through which individuals—aided by courts and data protection authorities—can suppress truthful information about themselves. Today, this framework is used primarily to delist embarrassing personal information and minor criminal records. But frameworks, once established, expand. The legal architecture of the right to be forgotten does not contain within itself a principled limit on the type of information that can be suppressed. It relies entirely on the discretionary judgment of regulators to prevent abuse. When that discretion fails—and it regularly does—truthful information is suppressed.

A free society is defined not by its ability to protect individuals from uncomfortable facts about themselves, but by its commitment to preserving the truth of what happened, even when that truth is inconvenient. The right to be forgotten asks us to abandon this commitment in the name of individual comfort. That is a price too high to pay.

Conclusion

The right to be forgotten is seductive because it promises something emotionally compelling: the chance to start over, to be judged not by the worst thing one has done but by the person one has become. These are admirable aspirations—but they should be pursued through personal growth, social grace, and the passage of time, not through legal mechanisms that suppress the truth.

An unrestricted historical record is not a burden on dignity; it is a foundation for accountability. The inability to escape one's documented past is not cruel—it is the natural consequence of living in a society that values transparency, truth, and the public's right to know. When we permit individuals to suppress truthful information about their public conduct, we do not create a kinder society. We create a society in which the past can be rewritten by those with the resources to do so, in which accountability can be escaped through legal procedure, and in which the collective memory is subject to individual whim.

The right to be forgotten should be opposed—not because we are indifferent to the suffering of those who bear the weight of an unflattering past, but because the cost of legal erasure is higher than the cost of legal memory. The truth, once publicly established, belongs to everyone. No court, no regulation, and no individual right should have the power to take it away.
